title: Honor the character
hook: girls flattered for looks from fourteen should learn they're honored for self-respect (Enchiridion 40)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the shoe that slides from gilded to purple to embroidered. Your line was the foot measures. Where did you notice enough? Day three hundred seventy-five.

Listen to what grown-ups say to children at a family party. To the little boys: you're so strong, you're so fast. To the little girls, again and again: look how pretty you are. It's meant kindly. But children pick up what the adults around them value, often from exactly these small remarks. Epictetus noticed the same thing in his own world, and wrote it down in a section of the handbook that's short, and a little uncomfortable, and still sharp. Today: honor the character.
screen: `STRONG, FAST. PRETTY.` → `CHILDREN LEARN WHAT WE VALUE.` → `HONOR THE CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: First, his world. In section forty Epictetus says that from about fourteen, girls are flattered by men and called ladies. Seeing that they're valued for nothing except their appeal to men, he says, they begin to dress up and put all their hopes in that. Second, his answer. It's worth taking care, he says, that they come to understand they're honored for nothing else than being decent and self-respecting. Not for looks. For character. That's the whole section. Third, an honest note. This chapter is written about girls, by a man, in a society that gave women little say over their own lives, and some modern readers find parts of its framing dated. But the core sentence points a finger at the people doing the flattering as much as at the girls, and it says plainly that a young woman's worth is in her character. Stoic teachers before him, like Musonius Rufus, Epictetus' own teacher, argued that women should study philosophy too. Fourth, why it reaches us. The praise we give teaches people what they're worth. Praise only looks, and you teach someone to put their hopes in a mirror, which time will eventually disappoint. Praise honesty, kindness, courage, effort, and you point them at the part of themselves nobody can take away. In Stoic terms, you praise what's up to them. That works for boys, for adults, for anyone. It just takes a little more attention than noticing a haircut.
screen: `FLATTERED FOR LOOKS FROM FOURTEEN.` · `HONORED FOR SELF-RESPECT.` · `DATED FRAME, SHARP CORE.` · `PRAISE WHAT'S UP TO THEM.` · then, large: `HONOR THE CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you'll see soon: a child, a friend, a coworker, a partner. Set aside how they look. Ask instead: what have I seen in their character lately? Patience with a hard customer. Honesty when it cost something. Kindness nobody else noticed. Find one, and find the words you'd use to name it, plainly. Hold those words ready. The bell holds the time.
Honor the character. Enchiridion forty: people should learn they're honored for decency and self-respect, not looks. Today's word.
Your line: honor the character. Praise one person today for character, not looks: name something they did that was up to them. Day three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism make a habit of praising others, especially children, for character and effort rather than appearance, following Epictetus' point in Enchiridion 40.

fork.setup: your niece shows you a drawing she worked on all afternoon, in a new dress. what fits Enchiridion 40?
options: you stuck with that all afternoon. tell me about it.
fork.reveal: he says people should learn they're honored for character, not looks. praise what was up to her.

original.note: Greek: self-respect, a sense of shame in the good sense. Enchiridion 40 uses the related adjective.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old rule about girls being modest.
what it means: people should learn they're honored for their character, not their looks, and the flatterers share the blame.
what a scholar hears: aidōs, self-respect, the quality Enchiridion 40 says they should be honored for; his teacher Musonius argued that women should study philosophy.

sources.ref: Musonius Rufus, Lecture 3 (that women too should study philosophy)

notes: Enchiridion 40 paraphrased: women from fourteen are called 'ladies' (kyriai) by men; seeing they have nothing else but to be bedded with men, they adorn themselves and place all hopes in that; it is worth attending that they perceive they are honored for nothing else than appearing decent/modest and self-respecting. The sexual phrasing is softened to 'valued for nothing except their appeal to men'. Confirm this is fair and appropriate for listeners of all ages.
The 'honest note' says many modern readers find the framing dated. Confirm tone.
Musonius Rufus, Lecture 3 ('That women too should study philosophy'); Musonius taught Epictetus. Confirm.
Greek: αἰδώς / αἰδήμων in Ench. 40. Confirm.
